title: Adverbial Participle Clauses with Prepositions and Reduced Clauses
summary: Combine prepositions with -ing clauses to express time, means, cause, accompanying circumstances and absence. Distinguish by, in, on, with and without, and use reduced conjunction and adjective clauses clearly without altering the implied subject or logical relationship.
learningObjectives: Use after, before, since, while and related prepositions with present or passive -ing clauses to express precise adverbial relationships.
Distinguish by + -ing for a means, on + -ing for a time point, and in + -ing for a circumstance, consequence or cause.
Select with + a subject + -ing and without + -ing for reasons, omitted actions, concessions and conditions.
Reduce suitable subject + be clauses after conjunctions or in adjective-led structures while preserving their meaning and reference.

explanation.heading: Prepositions followed by an -ing clause
explanation.body: After, before, since, while, through and similar prepositions can introduce a non-finite -ing clause. Unlike a finite clause, this clause has no tense of its own and usually shares an understood subject with the main clause. A passive reading needs being + past participle; where completed prior action needs extra emphasis, having + past participle may be possible after suitable prepositions, but it is often unnecessary after after. A finite clause is clearer when the subjects differ.
explanation.example: After reviewing the draft, Priya sent it to her colleagues.

explanation.heading: By, on and in are not interchangeable
explanation.body: By + -ing emphasises the method by which a result is achieved. On + -ing means when or immediately after an event, often in formal narration. In + -ing can describe the circumstances or the result of an action and sometimes the reason a speaker experienced something. The same verb can appear after by or in with a different focus; do not treat them as universal synonyms.
explanation.example: By reorganising the shelves, the team created space; on seeing the result, the manager smiled.

explanation.heading: With + subject + -ing; with + noun phrase
explanation.body: With can introduce a reason or accompanying circumstance. In a construction such as with the hall filling up, the subject the hall stands between with and the participle. With + noun phrase, including expressions such as with the roads closed, can also supply contextual reasons. This use is often less formal than a full because-clause; do not omit the explicit subject when it differs from the main-clause subject.
explanation.example: With the entrance getting crowded, the staff opened another door.

explanation.heading: Without + -ing: omission, concession or condition
explanation.body: Without + -ing frequently means that an action did not happen, but context can produce a concessive reading similar to although not or a conditional reading similar to unless. The intended interpretation must be made clear by the surrounding clause. In all cases, use an -ing form after without, not a bare infinitive or a finite clause without a separate connector.
explanation.example: Without checking the measurements, we cannot confirm the final dimensions.

explanation.heading: Reduced conjunction clauses and adjective phrases
explanation.body: In formal English, a conjunction followed by subject + be can sometimes be shortened by omitting the subject and be: while on duty; although disappointed; whenever possible. A fronted adjective phrase may similarly compress because someone was in a particular state. The missing subject or logical referent must remain recoverable; otherwise the shortened construction can imply that the wrong person is disappointed, absent or in danger.
explanation.example: Although disappointed by the outcome, the candidates thanked the organisers.

left.label: By + -ing: the method
left.example: By replacing the worn seal, the mechanic stopped the leak.
left.note: The replacement is presented as the means used to stop the leak.

right.label: In + -ing: circumstances or result
right.example: In replacing the worn seal, the mechanic discovered a cracked fitting.
right.note: The discovery occurred as part of the replacement process.

comparisons.title: An exact time relationship versus an ongoing situation

left.label: On + -ing: at the moment or immediately after
left.example: On entering the studio, Maya switched off her phone.
left.note: The phone was switched off at or just after the moment of entry.

right.label: While + -ing: during an ongoing action
right.example: While entering the studio, Maya noticed a loose cable.
right.note: Maya noticed the cable during the process of entering.

examples.sentence: Since moving to the coast, Tariq has cycled to work most days.
examples.note: Since + -ing marks a starting point for a situation continuing to the present.

examples.sentence: Before being published, the report was checked by two independent reviewers.
examples.note: Being + past participle makes the reduced clause passive.

examples.sentence: On hearing the announcement, the audience fell silent.
examples.note: On + -ing introduces an immediate time relationship.

examples.sentence: With the lift being repaired, deliveries have to use the stairs.
examples.note: The explicit subject the lift belongs to the with-clause, not to deliveries.

examples.sentence: Although unfamiliar with the system, Elise completed the task successfully.
examples.note: The implied subject of the reduced concessive clause is Elise.

commonMistakes.incorrect: By she checked the figures twice, she avoided an error.
commonMistakes.correct: By checking the figures twice, she avoided an error.
commonMistakes.why: A preposition such as by takes an -ing clause rather than a finite she checked clause in this structure.

commonMistakes.incorrect: On to receive the revised schedule, the volunteers called their teams.
commonMistakes.correct: On receiving the revised schedule, the volunteers called their teams.
commonMistakes.why: On marking immediate sequence is followed by an -ing form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: With the visitors were waiting outside, the guide opened the main gate.
commonMistakes.correct: With the visitors waiting outside, the guide opened the main gate.
commonMistakes.why: This with-absolute construction takes a subject plus -ing, not a finite were-clause.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Although disappointed about the result, the announcement was welcomed by the coach.
commonMistakes.correct: Although disappointed about the result, the coach welcomed the announcement.
commonMistakes.why: The shortened opening clause needs a matching human referent: the coach was disappointed, not the announcement.

studyTips: For each reduced clause, identify its logical subject and expand it into a full finite clause to check that you have kept the same people and events.
Write a three-way contrast with by replacing, in replacing and on replacing, and explain method, circumstance and moment of discovery.
When checking without clauses, paraphrase each one with without doing, although not doing or unless doing; retain only the reading that fits its context.

exercises.prompt: Which option shows how the technician solved the problem, not merely when it occurred? "___ the cable, she restored the connection."
exercises.feedback: By replacing identifies the replacement as the method used to restore the connection.

exercises.prompt: The curator made the discovery at the moment she opened the package. Choose the most precise opening: "___ the package, she noticed a missing label."
exercises.feedback: On opening marks the point at which she noticed the missing label.

exercises.prompt: The snow is falling now, and that explains the delay. Select the grammatical sentence.
choices: With the snow falling heavily, the trains are running late.
With the snow is falling heavily, the trains are running late.
With falling snow heavily, the trains are running late.
exercises.feedback: With the snow falling heavily gives the with-clause an explicit subject followed by -ing.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a reduced concessive phrase with a clear implied subject?
choices: Although tired, the report was finished by Elena.
Although tired, Elena finished the report.
Although Elena being tired, she finished the report.
exercises.feedback: Elena is the subject of finished and the person described as tired.

exercises.prompt: Complete the method phrase: ___ (review) the invoices one by one, the accountant found the discrepancy. Write the full phrase beginning with By.
exercises.feedback: By reviewing describes the method the accountant used.

exercises.prompt: Complete the time phrase: ___ (enter) the library, Omar remembered that he had forgotten his card. Begin with On.
exercises.feedback: On entering indicates when Omar remembered.

exercises.prompt: Complete the passive phrase: Before ___ (approve), every application receives a second check. Write the passive -ing form only.
exercises.feedback: Being approved makes the reduced before-clause passive; applications receive approval.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reduced condition: "We will answer follow-up questions ___ possible." Write one word.
exercises.feedback: Whenever possible reduces whenever it is possible.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: By to compare the two maps, Lina identified the missing street.
acceptedAnswers: By comparing the two maps, Lina identified the missing street.
exercises.feedback: A preposition requires the -ing form, so by comparing expresses means.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: With the audience was waiting quietly, the director began the speech.
acceptedAnswers: With the audience waiting quietly, the director began the speech.
exercises.feedback: A with-absolute construction can use the audience as its subject followed by waiting.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Without to check the final draft, I cannot approve its publication.
acceptedAnswers: Without checking the final draft, I cannot approve its publication.
exercises.feedback: Without takes a gerund, checking, not a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Correct the dangling modifier while preserving who was nervous: Although nervous, the presentation was delivered clearly by Imani.
acceptedAnswers: Although nervous, Imani delivered the presentation clearly.
exercises.feedback: The reduced adjective phrase must refer to Imani rather than the presentation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Transform these exact facts into one sentence showing means. Facts: The researcher consulted the archive. She found the original signature. Begin with "By consulting".
acceptedAnswers: By consulting the archive, the researcher found the original signature.
speakingExercises.feedback: By consulting expresses the method used to find the signature.

speakingExercises.prompt: Transform these facts to show an immediate moment: When Jonah opened the envelope, he recognised the handwriting. Begin with "On opening".
acceptedAnswers: On opening the envelope, Jonah recognised the handwriting.
speakingExercises.feedback: On opening replaces when he opened to mark the instant of discovery.

speakingExercises.prompt: Reduce this sentence to a passive -ing time phrase: Before the samples were tested, they were labelled. Begin with "Before being".
acceptedAnswers: Before being tested, the samples were labelled.
speakingExercises.feedback: Being tested retains the passive relationship; the samples were tested.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one sentence with an explicit with-clause subject. Facts: The lights / flicker; the staff / close the building. Begin with "With the lights".
acceptedAnswers: With the lights flickering, the staff closed the building.
speakingExercises.feedback: Lights is a separate subject inside the with-clause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence that expresses absence of an action. Facts: Nora left / she did not say goodbye. Begin with "Nora left".
speakingExercises.feedback: Without saying goodbye describes an action that did not occur.

speakingExercises.prompt: Reduce this concessive clause without changing the subject: Although she was uncertain, Leila signed the form. Begin with "Although".
acceptedAnswers: Although uncertain, Leila signed the form.
speakingExercises.feedback: Uncertain describes Leila, whose name follows as the main-clause subject.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the sentence aloud: "On receiving the news, the windows were opened by Karim." Make Karim the subject of the main clause.
acceptedAnswers: On receiving the news, Karim opened the windows.
speakingExercises.feedback: Karim, not the windows, received the news.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce two short sentences in order, preserving these exact facts. First: By practising daily / Eva / improved her timing. Second: On finishing the performance / Eva / smiled.
acceptedAnswers: By practising daily, Eva improved her timing. On finishing the performance, Eva smiled.
speakingExercises.feedback: By marks the method; on marks the time of the later reaction.

listeningExercises.audioText: By asking participants to explain their answers, the researchers discovered a flaw in the questionnaire.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the researchers discover the flaw in the questionnaire?
choices: By asking participants to explain their answers.
listeningExercises.feedback: The spoken by-clause states that asking participants was the means used.

listeningExercises.audioText: On reaching the entrance, the visitors realised that the gallery was closing.
listeningExercises.prompt: When did the visitors realise the gallery was closing?
choices: As they were buying tickets the previous day.
When they arrived at the entrance.
listeningExercises.feedback: On reaching the entrance locates the discovery at their arrival.

listeningExercises.audioText: After checking twice, the clerk signed the form.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the opening three-word time phrase.
listeningExercises.feedback: After checking twice marks an action completed before the clerk signed.

listeningExercises.audioText: With the wind getting stronger, the organisers closed the second entrance.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the reason for closing the second entrance?
listeningExercises.feedback: The with-clause explicitly gives the wind as the reason.

listeningExercises.audioText: Theo submitted the application without attaching the photograph.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did Theo fail to do before submitting his application?
listeningExercises.feedback: Without attaching the photograph specifies the omitted action.

listeningExercises.audioText: Although nervous about the questions, I continued the interview.
listeningExercises.prompt: Despite what feeling did the speaker continue the interview?
listeningExercises.feedback: Although nervous is a reduced concessive opening referring to the speaker.

listeningExercises.audioText: By sharing information, the two teams avoided duplicating the work.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the three-word phrase describing the method.
listeningExercises.feedback: By sharing information states how the teams avoided duplicated work.

listeningExercises.audioText: Without asking permission, the photographer entered the rehearsal room.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the opening three-word phrase describing an absent action.
listeningExercises.feedback: Without asking permission identifies the action that did not happen.
